title: Ogi, pickles and jam: preserving with acid and sugar

say: Ogi, pickles and jam: preserving with acid and sugar.
This is the video for module 3 of Food Preservation and Storage.
In a good ferment, friendly bacteria turn sugar into acid, and that sourness makes life hard for harmful bacteria.
Start by picking out stones and mouldy grains. Mouldy maize can carry aflatoxin, and souring does not remove it.

say: Steep the grain in plenty of safe water in a covered bucket, until a grain crushes easily. Ogi is almost all water, so safe water matters.

say: Cover it and let it settle and sour. Pour off the top water. The thick white sediment is ogi. Keep it under safe water changed daily, use a clean spoon, and use it within a few days.

say: A good ferment smells clean and pleasantly sour, is white or cream, and has clear water on top.

panel.heading: Good ferment or throw it away?

say: A rotten smell, coloured patches, slime or fuzzy mould means throw it away. Ferments that do not turn clearly sour, or that are sealed and kept warm, are risky. Do not invent fermented fish or meat products for sale.

panel.heading: Good ferment or throw it away?

say: In a pickle, acid is the safety line. Botulism bacteria will not grow below pH 4.6.
So use white vinegar of 5% acidity. Check the label, and never use vinegar of unknown strength.

panel.heading: Three pickling rules
items: Use vinegar of 5% acidity
Never change a tested recipe's proportions
Use pickling salt if salt is needed

say: Do not change the vinegar, water and vegetables in a tested recipe. Extra water or extra vegetables weaken the acid.

say: If the recipe asks for salt, use pickling salt. And wear gloves when cutting hot peppers.

say: For example, Ese sells pickled onion and carrot beside a suya spot in Benin City. Her card for 1 kg of vegetables uses 600 ml of vinegar and 400 ml of water.

panel.heading: Tripling a pickle without breaking it
items: 1 kg recipe: 600 ml vinegar, 400 ml water
Triple: 1,800 ml vinegar, 1,200 ml water
Vinegar stays 60% of the liquid
Extra litre of water: only 45%. Refused.

say: Jam works through three things. Pectin, a natural setting substance in fruit, forms the gel. Acid helps it set. Sugar ties up water so moulds cannot use it. Weigh your fruit and put a few saucers in the freezer.

panel.heading: Jam that sets and keeps
items: Weigh prepared fruit; chill a few saucers
Cook fruit soft; add lemon if low in pectin
Dissolve every sugar crystal on low heat
Boil hard, stirring often
Test on a cold saucer
Hot-fill hot sterilised jars, wipe rims, close

say: Cook the fruit soft. Pineapple and mango are low in pectin, so add lemon juice, or some guava or citrus.

say: Add the recipe's sugar and stir on low heat until every crystal dissolves, or the jam turns grainy.

say: Boil hard, stirring. Then drop a little on a cold saucer, wait a minute and push it. If it wrinkles, it is ready. If it runs, boil a few minutes more.

say: Boiling sugar is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Use a deep pot no more than half full and a long wooden spoon, and keep children away.

Throw away the whole jar. Mould threads grow below the surface you can see.

say: To remember. Ferment clean grain in safe water, and throw away anything mouldy or slimy. Pickle with 5% vinegar and never water it down. Keep pickles in the fridge unless processed by a tested method. And let the saucer test tell you when jam is ready.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Clean grain and safe water for every ferment
Pink, black or fuzzy mould: throw it away
5% vinegar, proportions never changed
Pickles in the fridge unless tested-processed
Pectin, acid and sugar make jam set and keep

say: Now practise. Make one batch of ogi and watch it for five days. Make a small fridge pickle with exact proportions. Then make a small batch of jam and work out the cost per jar.
